anchors.hint: the incoming axon/nerve fiber carrying the electrical signal into the terminal
the swollen end of the axon (the synaptic knob) where neurotransmitter is stored and released
mitochondrion inside the terminal, supplying ATP for the energy-demanding release process
voltage-gated calcium channel in the presynaptic membrane that opens when the action potential arrives
a synaptic vesicle storing neurotransmitter molecules before release
a vesicle fusing with the presynaptic membrane to release neurotransmitter (exocytosis)
the presynaptic cell membrane the vesicle fuses with
the fluid-filled gap the neurotransmitter diffuses across
an enzyme in the cleft (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) that breaks down neurotransmitter to stop the signal
the membrane of the next neuron, containing receptors
a receptor protein neurotransmitter binds to, opening an ion channel on the postsynaptic side
the next neuron/cell receiving and propagating the signal onward

templates.name: Nephron Cross-Section
templates.description: A labeled cross-section of a single nephron (renal corpuscle, proximal/distal convoluted tubules, loop of Henle, collecting duct) with the surrounding blood supply. Use for content describing kidney/nephron structure, ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, urine formation, or the role of ADH in water reabsorption.

anchors.hint: the vessel bringing blood into the glomerulus from the renal artery; wider than the efferent arteriole, which raises blood pressure inside the glomerulus

the tangled capillary knot inside Bowman's capsule; high blood pressure here forces water, ions, glucose, and other small molecules out of the blood (ultrafiltration) — blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through and stay in the blood
the cup-shaped capsule surrounding the glomerulus that collects the filtered fluid and funnels it into the tubule
the vessel carrying blood out of the glomerulus; narrower than the afferent arteriole, which keeps pressure inside the glomerulus high enough to keep filtering
the first coiled section of the tubule, where most reabsorption happens — essentially all glucose and amino acids, and most water, sodium and other ions, are reabsorbed back into the blood here
the descending limb of the loop of Henle; its wall is permeable to water, so as filtrate flows down into the increasingly salty medulla, water is drawn out by osmosis, concentrating the filtrate
the bend of the loop of Henle deep in the medulla, where the surrounding tissue fluid is most concentrated and the filtrate reaches its highest solute concentration

the ascending limb of the loop of Henle; its wall is impermeable to water but actively pumps sodium and chloride out into the surrounding tissue, diluting the filtrate and building the salt gradient that lets the collecting duct reabsorb water later
the second coiled section of the tubule, where further, hormonally-regulated reabsorption and secretion fine-tune the composition of the filtrate

the duct filtrate flows through on its way out of the kidney; antidiuretic hormone (ADH) makes its wall more permeable to water when the body needs to conserve water, so more water is reabsorbed here and less, more concentrated urine is produced
the network of capillaries wrapped around the tubule that picks up everything reabsorbed along the way and carries it back into the general blood circulation
